rationale: B wins because it keeps its hands on the actual facts and makes the unsupported parts explicit. Its “Mercury moves onto neobanks' turf with invite-only consumer accounts” is a clean competitive-entry story; A’s “Mercury Has 200,000 Business Customers. It Just Started Pitching Them Personally.” turns a possible distribution question into a claim the update does not support. A also opens with “Two Years After SVB,” which is calendar malpractice in June 2026.
gaps_in_A: “Two Years After SVB” is factually wrong. SVB collapsed in March 2023; by June 9, 2026, this is more than three years later.

“Mercury's name recognition was built entirely on being the startup-banking alternative” overstates the supplied fact. The update says Mercury became well known after SVB, not that its recognition was built entirely there.

“It Just Started Pitching Them Personally” is unsupported. The facts say Mercury serves 200,000 businesses and has an invite-only waitlist; they do not say existing business customers are being pitched or invited first.
“Mercury's playbook runs opposite to the consumer-to-business neobank trajectory most competitors have tried” imports a market thesis not present in the update.
gaps_in_B: “Mercury says it's profitable on 200,000 businesses” compresses two separate facts into a slightly too-neat economics claim. The update says Mercury says it is profitable and serves over 200,000 businesses; it does not tie profitability to that base.
“Consumer banking will test that claim” is a useful scrutiny frame, but it needs sharper proof before pitching because consumer economics, pricing, and deposit targets are all undisclosed.

“Mercury wants to hold consumers' money without being a bank” is punchy but should be handled carefully because the update says partner banks provide the banking services; the angle later clarifies this, but the headline risks sounding more accusatory than precise.
